extracted.intended_audience: educated reading public interested in literature, theatre, and manners (early-18th-century Spectator readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing/criticizing Spectator-style periodical essays on poetry, theatre, and social conduct — covering use of allegory/personification, what makes a pleasant companion (humour), dress/appearance as social strategy, and theatrical devices like the cat-call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of principal parts in a heroick poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroick poem 'ought to appear credible in its principal Parts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ornament and sublime imagination are valuable, the main actions and agents of a heroic poem must remain plausible and credible to the reader; devices that strain credulity weaken a heroic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imaginary persons as short allegorical figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Short Allegories (imaginary Persons) are 'very beautiful in Poetry when they are just shewn, without being engaged in any Series of Action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personifications used briefly to convey a particular circumstance (e.g., 'Victory sat on the right Hand') are effective poetic phrases rather than full allegorical descriptions; such short uses are appropriate and charming (Homer, Virgil, Milton examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making imaginary persons primary actors
rubrics_metrics.description: When imaginary Persons 'are introduced as principal Actors, and engaged in a Series of Adventures, they take too much upon them, and are by no means proper for an Heroick Poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not center the plot of a heroic poem on allegorical figures (e.g., Sin and Death as active agents). Extended personified characters engaged in adventures reduce credibility and are inappropriate for the heroic genre; reserve them for other kinds of composition or brief emblematic uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apt diction for describing allegorical action
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reader 'who knows the Strength of the English Tongue, will be amazed to think how the Poet could find such apt Words and Phrases to describe the Action[s] of those two imaginary Persons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using personification or allegory, select language finely tuned to the actions and qualities described; apt words and phrases can make even shadowy figures vivid and moving when used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification in sublime writings: restraint and grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: In sublime writings (e.g., Scripture), brief mention of an imaginary Person 'has something in it more just, as well as great, than all that the most fanciful Poet could have bestowed upon her.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sublime or prophetic effects, a restrained, terse personification (a single evocative phrase) can be more powerful and appropriate than elaborate poetic embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a pleasant companion (the Frolick)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Frolick 'is the Play of the Mind, and consists of various and unforced Sallies of Imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasant company arises from a judicious mix of qualities: tasteful, unforced wit; the ability to descend agreeably from decorum; lively but not offensive gestures; and contributions that neither over-dominate nor embarrass others. Festivity of spirit should feel natural, not forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loud, mischievous, or injurious merriment
rubrics_metrics.description: Loud, mischievous, airy, dull companions are mistaken in what they call a Frolick; many jokers 'do Things which do not become them' and add 'something mischievous to themselves or others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include destructive or hazardous jests (e.g., drawing teeth, burning clothing, public indecency) and ostentatious displays of humour that cause harm or shame. True humour should avoid inflicting distress or scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine frolickry to the place of meeting (analogy to unity of time/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be amiss if all who pretend to be Companions 'would confine their Action to the Place of Meeting: For a Frolick carried farther may be better performed by other Animals than Men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep jests and merriment appropriate to context and company; avoid carrying pranks beyond the social bounds of the gathering where they are understood and acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimickry should preserve the dignity of the represented
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mimick 'has a Mimickry that does not debase the Person he represents; but which, taking from the Gravity of the Character, adds to the Agreeableness of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative humour should tease or lighten a subject without humiliating or degrading it; skillful gesture and representation can make even serious subjects agreeable when handled with tact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in dress as social strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearing in a better Dress is sometimes 'pardonable but necessary' to gain access to higher company; the author defends 'two plain Suits a Year' and recommends modest appearance to aid social advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress matters because most people judge by appearance before they judge learning or character. Young men of limited means may reasonably invest in modest yet genteel clothing to secure opportunities, but should avoid extravagant foppery or spending beyond means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance leisure, study, and social polish
rubrics_metrics.description: While appearance and acquaintance matter, 'the gross of [a young fellow's] Time ought to be sacred to more substantial Acquisitions' and he should not spend more time or money than his studies or means require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate learning and profession first; use modest social polish (dress, measured conversation) to open doors, but keep primary devotion to study and steady professional progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cat-call as a theatrical instrument (appropriate uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cat-call 'is peculiarly appropriated to the Stage: It very much Improves the Sound of Nonsense, and often goes along with the Voice of the Actor... It has often supplied the Place of the antient Chorus... a bad Poet has as great an Antipathy to a Cat-call.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cat-call is an instrument of theatrical criticism and audience response: use it on stage to express disapproval of poor writing or performance, to punctuate comic or tragic moments as a shared critical device, and to accompany the actor's voice when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper uses of the cat-call
rubrics_metrics.description: The author 'can by no means approve the Thought' of using the cat-call outside the theatre (example: an angry lover using it in a serenade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using theatrical instruments like the cat-call in private or romantic settings; their dramatic, mocking, or derisive character makes them unsuitable and offensive outside the stage context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cat-call as a coded criticism with distinct notes
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist 'teaches to play on it by Book, and to express by it the whole Art of Criticism. He has his Base and his Treble Cat-call... a particular Squeak to denote the Violation of each of the Unities, and has different Sounds to shew whether he aims at the Poet or the Player... the Smut-note, the Fustian-note, the Stupid-note.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the stage, the cat-call may be used with a repertoire of distinct sounds to convey specific critical judgments (e.g., criticism of plot unities, of poetical faults, or of actor performance). If adopting such devices, make the code intelligible and proportionate to the fault being signalled.
